records.quote:
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Syntax::

  capture_pattern: !"_" NAME

The single underscore (``_``) is not a capture pattern (this is what
``!"_"`` expresses).  It is treated as a `wildcard pattern`_.

A capture pattern always succeeds.  It binds the subject value to the
name using the scoping rules for name binding established for the
walrus operator in :pep:`572`.  (Summary: the name becomes a local
variable in the closest containing function scope unless there's an
applicable ``nonlocal`` or ``global`` statement.)

In a given pattern, a given name may be bound only once.  This
disallows for example ``case x, x: ...`` but allows ``case [x] | x:
...``.


.. _634-wildcard_pattern:

Wildcard Pattern
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Syntax::

    wildcard_pattern: "_"

A wildcard pattern always succeeds.  It binds no name.


Value Patterns
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
records.statement: A Python wildcard pattern always succeeds and binds no name; underscore is not a capture pattern.
records.subject: Python wildcard pattern bindings
records.scope: Python match patterns; not ordinary underscore assignments

records.quote:
Name bindings made during a successful pattern match outlive the
executed block and can be used after the match statement.

During failed pattern matches, some subpatterns may succeed. For
example, while matching the pattern ``(0, x, 1)`` with the value ``[0,
1, 2]``, the subpattern ``x`` may succeed if the list elements are
matched from left to right.  The implementation may choose to either
make persistent bindings for those partial matches or not. User code
including a match statement should not rely on the bindings being
made for a failed match, but also shouldn't assume that variables are
unchanged by a failed match.  This part of the behavior is left
intentionally unspecified so different implementations can add
optimizations, and to prevent introducing semantic restrictions that
could limit the extensibility of this feature.
records.statement: Failed Python pattern matches leave partial name bindings intentionally unspecified: assume neither binding nor preservation.
records.subject: Python failed pattern bindings
records.scope: Python failed match statements; partial bindings only

records.quote:
It is intended that programs written to the Go 1 specification will continue to compile and run correctly, unchanged, over the lifetime of that specification. At some indefinite point, a Go 2 specification may arise, but until that time, Go programs that work today should continue to work even as future "point" releases of Go 1 arise (Go 1.1, Go 1.2, etc.).

Compatibility is at the source level. Binary compatibility for compiled packages is not guaranteed between releases. After a point release, Go source will need to be recompiled to link against the new release.
records.statement: Go 1 compatibility is intended at source level; binary compatibility between releases is not guaranteed and relinking requires recompilation.
records.subject: Go source binary compatibility
records.scope: Go 1 specification and standard packages; source compatibility between releases

status_evidence.quote:

At some indefinite point, a Go 2 specification may arise, but until that time, Go programs that work today should continue to work even as future "point" releases of Go 1 arise (Go 1.1, Go 1.2, etc.).

records.quote:
Although we expect that the vast majority of programs will maintain this compatibility over time, it is impossible to guarantee that no future change will break any program. This document is an attempt to set expectations for the compatibility of Go 1 software in the future. There are a number of ways in which a program that compiles and runs today may fail to do so after a future point release. They are all unlikely but worth recording.

  • Security. A security issue in the specification or implementation may come to light whose resolution requires breaking compatibility. We reserve the right to address such security issues.
records.statement: Go compatibility expectations allow breaking compatibility to address security issues; they cannot guarantee every program.
records.subject: Go security compatibility exception
records.scope: Go specification or implementation security issues requiring incompatible resolution

status_evidence.quote: Security. A security issue in the specification or implementation may come to light whose resolution requires breaking compatibility. We reserve the right to address such security issues.

records.quote: • Struct literals. For the addition of features in later point releases, it may be necessary to add fields to exported structs in the API. Code that uses unkeyed struct literals (such as pkg.T{3, "x"}) to create values of these types would fail to compile after such a change. However, code that uses keyed literals (pkg.T{A: 3, B: "x"}) will continue to compile after such a change. We will update such data structures in a way that allows keyed struct literals to remain compatible, although unkeyed literals may fail to compile. (There are also more intricate cases involving nested data structures or interfaces, but they have the same resolution.) We therefore recommend that composite literals whose type is defined in a separate package should use the keyed notation.
records.statement: Go exported structs may gain fields: unkeyed literals can fail, while keyed literals remain compatible with such additions.
records.subject: Go keyed unkeyed struct literals
records.scope: Go exported API structs defined in another package; added fields

status_evidence.quote: • Struct literals. For the addition of features in later point releases, it may be necessary to add fields to exported structs in the API. Code that uses unkeyed struct literals (such as pkg.T{3, "x"}) to create values of these types would fail to compile after such a change. However, code that uses keyed literals (pkg.T{A: 3, B: "x"}) will continue to compile after such a change. We will update such data structures in a way that allows keyed struct literals to remain compatible, although unkeyed literals may fail to compile. (There are also more intricate cases involving nested data structures or interfaces, but they have the same resolution.) We therefore recommend that composite literals whose type is defined in a separate package should use the keyed notation.

records.quote: Finally, although it is not a correctness issue, it is possible that the performance of a program may be affected by changes in the implementation of the compilers or libraries upon which it depends. No guarantee can be made about the performance of a given program between releases.
records.statement: Go makes no guarantee about a given program performance between releases.
records.subject: Go performance compatibility guarantee
records.scope: Performance of a given Go program across releases

cases.task: Which Python pattern matching specification replaces PEP 622?
included_conditions: Retain both the superseded source and its explicit replacement; Final is mapped to documentary acceptance.
negative_cases: Do not promote PEP 622 to current policy.

cases.task: May Python use the PEP 640 unused variable syntax instead of wildcard patterns?
included_conditions: Steering Council rejection survives alongside the final wildcard specification.
negative_cases: A prototype is not acceptance; underscore is special only as a wildcard pattern.
must_remain_unknown: Whether any fork implements the rejected syntax.

cases.task: Can Python failed pattern matches guarantee that partial bindings are unchanged?
included_conditions: Assume neither persistent partial bindings nor unchanged variables after failure.
negative_cases: Do not generalize successful match binding behavior to failed matches.
must_remain_unknown: Which bindings a particular interpreter preserves on a failed match.

cases.task: Does Go source compatibility guarantee binary compatibility between releases?
included_conditions: Retain intended source compatibility and the binary/recompilation qualification together.
negative_cases: Source compatibility is not a binary ABI promise.
must_remain_unknown: Whether a particular binary links or runs.

cases.task: Does Go compatibility prevent a breaking security fix?
included_conditions: Security issues may justify incompatible fixes; the general expectation is qualified.
negative_cases: The exception does not authorize arbitrary unrelated breaking changes.
must_remain_unknown: Whether a particular fix is necessary or deployed.

cases.task: Can Go add exported struct fields without preserving unkeyed literals?
included_conditions: Retain both keyed compatibility and unkeyed failure under field additions.
negative_cases: Do not claim every composite literal is incompatible or every unkeyed literal protected.
must_remain_unknown: Whether a specific upstream struct gained a field.

cases.task: Does Go performance compatibility guarantee unchanged latency between releases?
included_conditions: No guarantee of performance for a given program between releases.
negative_cases: A compatibility policy is not a measured latency regression.
must_remain_unknown: Performance, measurements and causation for any concrete program.
